Impact of micro-aerobic conditions in UASB Reactor using media to improve the 
removal efficiency of organics and nutrients from wastewater
Mahmood Ahmada, Aaqib Ashraf Sheikha, Mohammad Ishteyaque Ahmada, Farooq Ahmad Wania, Beni Lewb
and Abid Ali Khana
aDepartment of Civil Engineering, Jamia Millia Islamia (A Central University), New Delhi, India; bDepartment of Civil Engineering, 
Ariel University, Ariel, Israel
ABSTRACT  
The present study attempted to investigate the impact of the micro-aerobic condition in a 
conventional Up-Flow Anaerobic Sludge Blanket Reactor (UASB) using different media for the 
treatment of municipal wastewater. The Hydraulic Retention Time (HRT), Dissolved Oxygen (DO), 
intermittent and continuous aeration were the important operating conditions of this study 
carried out for more than 1015 days. Fourier transform infra red (FTIR) spectra and SEM analysis 
indicate the significant growth of the microbiota responsible for the removal of nutrients. 
Significant increase in the removal of the chemical oxygen demand (COD)∼ 91%, biochemical 
oxygen demand (BOD)∼ 90%, suspended solids (SS)∼ 92%, and ammonical nitrogen (NH4
+–N)∼ 
90%, were observed at lower DO levels. Sulphate was dominant due to sulphide oxidation 
during micro-aerobic conditions in almost all study phases, which resulted in an increase of up 
to 90% of the influent sulphates. The micro-aerobic UASB process could be a feasible option for 
achieving the latest treated effluent disposal norms and significantly reducing the energy 
demand for wastewater treatment.

KEYWORDS  
Micro-aerobic UASB system; 
HRT; DO; sewage
1 Introduction
The application of biological processes for the removal 
of organics, phosphorus, and nitrogenous compounds 
from municipal wastewater is extensively reported in 
the literature. The treatment efficiency of these pro­
cesses depends on the different parameters and tech­
nology [1,2]. Usually, anaerobic systems are not as 
efficient as aerobic processes for the removal of organics 
from the wastewater [3,4], predominantly operated at 
small hydraulic retention times (HRT <10 h) [5].
The up-flow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactor 
has been used for a long time to clean wastewater in 
developing countries, especially tropical ones like India, 
Brazil, Colombia, and China [6]. Since the UASB is a robust 
technology, it’s imperative to investigate the approaches 
to modify the UASB process and enhance the elimination 
of organics and nutrients from municipal wastewater, 
specifically designed for short HRTs (usually less than 8 h). 
Micro-aerating the anaerobic reactors, which means 
adding little amounts of O2 (up to 1–2 mg O2 L−1), may 
be a better option in this case and may be easier to run 
and cost less [7], to make it easier for bacteria that make 
monooxygenase to break down compounds that are 
hard to break down, like aromatic hydrocarbons [8].

It has already been shown that this method makes it 
much easier to get rid of organic matter and nutrients 
in an anaerobic reactor with no affecting its general 
performance or stability [9]. Though the earlier study 
only looked at a single airflow rate (1 mL min−1 at 27 
oC and 1 atm, which is the same as 0.021 L O2 L−1 
feed). Because of this, the amount of O2 used was 
much lower than the maximum of 1 L O2 L−1 feed 
[10]. This means that higher microaeration flow rates 
could be used to make the removal of organic matter 
and nutrients even more effective in anaerobic 
reactors.
However, if there is more O2 in the system, it may 
prevent the methanogenic activity, which is said to be 
directly related to the anaerobic biotransformation of 
organic compounds [11].
Thus, testing various airflow rates is important to find 
out the limits of this engineering approach in terms of 
both system stability and efficiency. This will help 
prove microaeration as a useful technology that can 
be used in large anaerobic systems to help them get 
rid of more organic matter and nutrients. Presently, 
limited studied found in the literature on micro-aeration 
of UASB for sewage treatment.
Hence, this study aimed to evaluate the effect of 
PVA-Gel and Zeolite as bio media to improve the 
removal of organics and nutrients from municipal 
wastewater. The existing UASB process was modified 
to a Micro-Aerobic UASB process by injecting micro- 
aeration in the upper zone of the reactor. Micro aeration 
was verified to be an effective approach to improve the 
biotransformation/ removal of the organics and nutri­
ents at short HRT.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Wastewater feed, seed sludge and biomass 
carrier
The sewage was brought daily from the nearby inter­
mediate pumping station (IPS) and filled in a 1000 L 
capacity tank kept in the premises of the laboratory of 
microbial technologies for upgradation of anaerobic 
processes (Labmite), Department of Civil Engineering, 
Jamia Millia Islamia (A Central University), New Delhi. 
The anaerobic sludge was obtained from UASB based 
sewage treatment plant (STP) of capacity 111 million 
litres per day (MLD), Ludhiana, India.
The TS (Total Solids) and VS (Volatile Solids) of 
anaerobic sludge were 58 and 43 g L−1, respectively. 
The PVA Gel and Zeolite were used simultaneously as 
the biomass carriers at a 30–40% reactor volume 
ratio. The bio media was utilised to develop the 
accessibility of the microorganism population to 
settle in and reduce the effect of outer environmental 
conditions.
2.2. Experimental set-up and operating 
conditions
2.2.1. Continuous flow studies
The continuous flow experiment was performed in a 
Micro-Aerobic UASB reactor fabricated from Perspex 
material having a working volume of 38 L at an HRT of 
6 h. The reactor was fed with the municipal wastewater 
by a peristaltic pump (Miclins) brought daily from the 
nearby sewage pumping station (SPS), Batla House, 
New Delhi, India, and operated at a room temperature 
varied from 15 to 32 0C.
A micro-porous aeration device and rotâmeter were 
used to adjust the aeration flow rate of 100–200 mL/ 
min to maintain DO levels between 0.5 and 2.5 mg/L. 
The micro-porous tube was made of polyethylene 
(pore size: 2.5 mm), and the aeration tube was con­
nected to the air pump and was placed in the middle 
of the reactor above the sludge bed with recirculation 
at the bottom. The biogas produced was collected in a 
gas holder.
The present study was divided into two phases as 
summarised in Table S1. Initially, in phase 1 with inter­
mittent aeration, the major focus of the study was on 
the removal of the dissimilar organics and nutrients 
under anaerobic conditions, which extends to explore 
the consequence of micro-aeration on the biotrans­
formation/ removal of organics and nutrients at DO 
levels of 1.0–2.0 mg/L under operating conditions 1– 
3. Subsequently, under operating conditions 4-5, the 
adaptation of the microbiota under microaerobic con­
ditions was evaluated. Although the stabilised concen­
tration was achieved at each stage, the average 
effluent COD consistently decreased throughout all 
phases.
In phase 2, the effect of continuous micro-aeration on 
the removal/biotransformation of organics and nutrients 
at DO<1.0–2.0 mg/L under conditions 1–2 at HRT 
30 min. Condition 3 concludes the experiment by rein­
forcing the oxygen effect and disproving the idea of 
microbial adaptability. The reactor was again operated 
at DO 1.0–1.5 mg/L with recycle in the aerobic zone, 
and in condition 4, the reactor was operated at the 
same DO but with recycle in the anaerobic zone. The 
experimental conditions were changed after verifying 
system stability with the average effluent COD, BOD 
and nutrient removal consistently decreased throughout 
the phase.

2.2.2. Batch studies
Experiments were also conducted in the batch reactors 
[100 mL serum bottles] for more than 60 days to culti­
vate the AnAOB (anaerobic ammonium-oxidising bac­
teria) and POAs (phosphorus-accumulating organisms) 
using different seed sludge and media. The present 
study was started with a synthetic feed to optimise the 
doses and operating conditions. The aerobic sludge 
was collected from the STP [see Section 2.1]. PVA Gel 
and Zeolite were used as the media for the attached 
growth of biomass. The media i.e. PVA-Gel and Zeolite 
were inoculated with aerobic and anaerobic sludge. 
The ratio of sludge to media was kept 1:1 on a weight 
basis. The 3 g/L of sludge along with 3 g/L of attached 
media were introduced in a batch reactor and kept at 
a constant temperature of 35 ± 2 °C. The agitation/ or 
mixing of sludge was done during the batch feeding 
of all reactors. All these batch reactors were operated 
in sequencing batch mode, where a hydraulic retention 
time of 3 d was maintained. The study was divided into 
eight phases [Table S2]. Each phase was planned to con­
tinue until the observation of stable performance was 
observed based on NH4
+-N concentration. I stage 
begins with 50 mg/L supplement of NH4
+-N followed by 
an increment up to 100 mg/L NH4
+-N supplement in II 
stage. Subsequently, nitrite was introduced in the syn­
thetic feed in stages III, IV, and V in the increasing 
order of 25, 50, and 100 mg/L, respectively. In stages 
VI, VII, and VIII, carbon was supplemented with synthetic 
wastewater to maintain ammonia: COD (chemical 
oxygen demand) ratios of 1:1, 1:1:5, and 1:2 to investi­
gate the effect of carbon on enriched ammonia-oxidis­
ing bacteria.
2.3. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was con­
ducted to assess the chemical and structural properties 
of sludge samples at the start and conclusion of the 
study (0 and 1015 days) utilising a Bruker, USA (Model; 
Tensor; 37) at the Central Instrumentation Facility, 
Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi. Samples were prepared 
in accordance with the instrumental methodology. The 
operational range employed was 4000–600 cm−1, with 
a resolution of 10 cm−1.
2.4. SEM analysis
Ten millilitres of sludge were put on a poly-L-lysine- 
coated glass slide and left to dry in the air. After that, 
2.5% glutaraldehyde was used to fix the samples for 
24 h at 4 °C. With phosphate buffer (pH 7.4), the fixed 
samples were centrifuged at 4000 rpm for one minute. 
The supernatant was then thrown away. For dehydrating 
the sample, analytical grade ethanol mixed with double- 
distilled water was used. The sample was then dried in a 
hot air oven at 110 °C. The samples were covered with 
100 nm of gold and looked at with a scanning electron 
microscope (ZEISS ΣIGMA, Germany) at the Center for 
Nanoscience & Nanotechnology, Jamia Millia Islamia, 
New Delhi, to confirm the morphology of sludge.
2.5. Analytical procedure
All the physico-chemical parameters were analysed 
according to the Standard Methods of examination of 
water and wastewater (APHA, 18th ed, 1992).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Batch study
3.1.1. Removal of Nitrogen and phosphorus 
without the use of media
Figure S1 depicts the variation of nitrogen and phos­
phorus levels during phases I and II of the investigation, 
in both aerobic and anaerobic sludge without any 
associated media. The results indicate that the elimin­
ation of NH4
+-N increased from 17 to 25% over the first 
9 days and continued to grow up to 86–94%  at the 
end of the study phase I (day 30).
During phase II, it was noted that the efficacy of NH4
+- 
N removal steadily decreased to 50% by day 48 and 
further decreased to 17–25% by the conclusion of 
phase II (day 60). In the aerobic sludge, the process of 
nitrification showed a progressive increase for the first 
9 days. However, no additional nitrification was seen 
during phase I. However, at the same concentration 
of ammonium, the process of nitrification increases in 
the effluent at the end of phase 1. In a similar 
manner, the accumulation of nitrite was not observed 
until day 13, after which it gradually decreased until 
day 55 (phase II). Subsequently, as the efficacy of 
NH4
+-N removal increases, the accumulation of nitrite 
similarly rises up. Due to partial oxidation to nitrate 
(denitrification), the observed trend indicates that 
increased NH4
+-N removal efficiency encourages nitrite 
build-up. However, denitrification was not observed 
in phase I of the anaerobic sludge due to the absence 
of oxygen.
During phase II, the process of nitrification experi­
enced a rise and reached levels ranging from 2 to 
18 mg/L. Nitrite concentration was first seen on day 13 
during phase I and thereafter peaked at levels ranging 
from 10 to 22 mg/L during phase II. At the conclusion

3.2. Continuous study
3.2.1. Temporal variation of organics
The reactor effluent COD was consistently low, with con­
centrations of 75–85 mg/L in phase 1 and 80–91 mg/L in 
phase 2, respectively. The results indicate significant 
efficiency in the flocculation or granulation of waste­
water colloidal substances, promising the reactor’s 
optimal functionality regarding organic compound oxi­
dation and biomass proliferation. Despite the fact that 
a stabilised concentration was achieved at each stage, 
the average effluent COD consistently decreased 
throughout all phases. In phase 2, effluent COD 
reached levels anticipated for this high-efficiency treat­
ment modality with a COD removal rate of 91%, as illus­
trated in Figures 1 and 2. A previous study has shown the 
removal of dissolved methane via an air stripper [12]. 
This study evaluated the potential outcomes for dis­
solved methane within the UASB, encompassing dega­
sification via off-gas from the media sludge, stripping 
to the gas phase under mixing or scouring conditions, 
and biological oxidation by methane-oxidising bacteria 
(MOB) or methanotrophs. The effluent dissolved 
methane concentration ranged from 34 to 51 mg/L 
(±0.9) throughout this investigation. Methane was unde­
tected in the headspace examination of aqueous UASB

dition 3–4 in phase 2.

portion of the media in the UASB reactor, likely due to 
the oxidation of CH4 by methanotrophic organisms or 
organic materials by heterotrophic bacteria. The sup­
plementary aerobic heterotrophic degradation of 
soluble organic molecules was assessed by measuring 
the COD of UASB influent and effluent samples. UASB 
effluent samples were filtered using Whatman filter 
paper to quantify soluble COD following the elimination 
of solids generated by microbial action e.g. detached bio 
media; EPS (extracellular polymeric substances). The 
influent COD of the UASB was 310–500 (±10) mg/L, 
whereas the effluent COD was 80–91 mg/L, demonstrat­
ing a COD removal efficiency of 91% by the UASB 
system. The UASB effluent exhibited a TSS content of 
less than 128–129 mg/L in phases 1 and 2, thereby com­
plying with the secondary effluent quality standards 
established by the USEPA, with a removal efficiency of 
92%, as illustrated in Figure 1. The COD for the oxidation 
of sulphides and dissolved CH4 was each less than 
91 mg/L, with a removal efficiency of 91%, as illustrated 
in Figures S4–S5. The observed BOD values during the 
continuous 
study 
were 
lesser 
for 
nitrification 
(∼200 mg/L), suggesting that CH4 and sulphide-oxidis­
ing bacteria exceed for nitrifiers in oxygen utilisation, 
hence showing that the activity of nitrifiers was probably 
controlled by oxygen availability.
3.2.2. Temporal variation of sulphates and 
sulphides
The UASB influent SO4
2− and H2S concentrations was less 
than 85 mg/L (±1) before micro-aeration (Figure 3). After 
treatment with media with intermittent and continuous 
aeration in phases 1 and 2, the effluent SO4
2− concen­
trations and removal effectiveness were not affected 
by variations of DO and were observed as 20–45 mg/L. 
The removal efficiency of sulphate was 65–70%. The 
SO4
2− was completely separated by oxidation as it 
diffused into biofilms mounting on media installed in a 
reactor. This resulted in the swift elimination of sulphate 
and sulphide after the micro-aeration during phase 1 
[condition 1–5] when the H2S loading rate was less than 
2.0 mg/L. During phase 2, when continuous aeration 
was given with recycling in the anaerobic zone and 
mixing (Figure 4), the sulphate decreased from 85 to 
10 mg/L and gets further lowered due to decreased 
mixing between dissolved SO4
2− and sulphur-oxidising 
bacteria (SOB).
The H2S was detected in the UASB effluent at concen­
trations below 2 mg/L during phase 1. This data suggests 
that SOB eliminated sulphide within the plastic carrier 
situated in the anaerobic zone. Sulphate constituted the 
predominant sulphide oxidation product across all 
stages, representing over 90% of the influent sulphide, 
and its effluent removal diminished with continuous aera­
tion. Particulate elemental sulphur raised concerns due to 
its contribution to effluent turbidity.
3.2.3. Temporal variation of NH4-N
In contrast to the high sulphate removal efficiency talked 
about earlier, the UASB removed 85% of the ammonia in 
phase 2, and this number changed based on the operat­
ing conditions, as shown in Figure 4. The system was 
75% effective at getting rid of ammonia when the 
ammonia concentration was 14 mg/L in phase 2 (con­
dition 3–4). The removal efficiency dropped to 10% in 
phase 2 when the ammonia loading rate was 9 mg/L. 
This was because of the recycling and constant micro- 
aeration. In phase 2 [condition 3–4], the biofilm that 
formed on the media got thicker, which could mean 
that the nitrifiers stayed on the biofilm longer. When 
biofilm thickness was used as a media, the ammonia 
removal rate went up from 85% to 90% at the same 
ammonia influent concentration. The highest concen­
tration of ammonia removed was 9 mg/L (Figure 3). 
Based on these results, it is possible that nitrifiers 
could grow on the outside of the biofilm. In Phase 2 
[condition 4], the ability to remove ammonia was 
lowered by 86% to help a thicker biofilm grow by redu­
cing 
turbulence. 
The 
NH4
+-N 
removal 
efficiency 
decreased largely due to limited contact of NH4
+ with 
nitrifiers [13]. In phase 2, continual micro-aeration 
under restricted mixing conditions, coupled with elev­
ated nitrogen concentration in the influent, resulted in 
a further decline in efficiency. Ammonia in effluent and 
its oxidation products, such as nitrate was major pro­
ducts formed. The nitrate concentration in the influent 
was 2–3 mg/L prior to micro-aeration and increased to 
4–6 mg/L in the effluent following micro-aeration. The 
efficacy of controlled ammonia removal varies from 
earlier lab-scale UASB research that accomplished simul­
taneous nitrification and anoxic sulphide oxidation. Both 
studies found that Nitrospira mostly oxidised ammonia 
to nitrate, then denitrified via the combination of sul­
phide oxidation with nitrate reduction enabled by Thio­
bacillus. Two-layer biofilms consisting of nitrifiers in the 
inner aerobic biofilm adjacent to the membranes with 
accessible oxygen and anoxic sulphide-oxidising bac­
teria on the outer biofilm where oxygen is limited, 
with nitrate reduction possibly producing sulphate or 
elemental sulphur, may be features of the lab-scale 
UASB. This work shows that aerobic respiration was pre­
ferred over nitrification in terms of sulphide removal, 
implying that aerobic SOBs dominated UASB biofilms 
and hence limited O2 availability for nitrifiers. Neverthe­
less, it is noteworthy that variations in O2 permeability

3.2.4. Temporal variation of PO4-P
The UASB reactor with a microaerobic reaction phase 
was not intended for phosphorus removal. Conse­
quently, in phase 1, phosphorus was predominantly 
eliminated to satisfy the metabolic requirements of het­
erotrophic species. In phase 2 setups, which include 
recycling in the anaerobic zone, the metabolic selection 
of slow-growing organisms, such as PAOs (poly-phos­
phate accumulating organisms) or DPAOs (denitrifying 
phosphate-accumulating organisms), was facilitated. 
PAOs are preferentially favoured at elevated P/COD 
ratios, whereas DPAOs exhibit enhanced development 
at reduced P/COD ratios [16]. Both PAOs and DPAOs 
assimilate COD under anaerobic circumstances, which 
benefit in energy conservation due to the lack of air 
supplies, in contrast to a completely aerobic grainy 
sludge reactor. Continuous microaerobic conditions 
were seen to effectively remove biologically available 
phosphorus in domestic wastewater, with levels exceed­
ing 2 mg/L, which is approximately the minimum 
threshold necessary for phosphorus removal, as illus­
trated in Figure 4. As a result, the accumulation of 
PAOs was restricted, leading to the proliferation of 
DPAOs. It was anticipated that PAOs activity facilitated 
phosphorus removal in both phases, serving as the 
primary 
mechanism 
for 
phosphorus 
elimination 
throughout both stages of heterotrophic development. 
The involvement of other organisms liable for phos­
phorus removal, different from Accumulibacter, such as 
Tetrasphaera [17], which grows when the wastewater 
contains complex substrates. Beginning with phase 1, 
the phosphorus elimination attributable to PAO activity 
was minimal according to mass balances. The results 
indicate that PAOs exhibit significant sensitivity to oper­
ational conditions, as corroborated by recent studies 
from other authors [18]. It was the combination of a 
low P/COD ratio and micro-aeration feeding variations 
that inhibited PAOs.
3.3. FTIR characterisation and surface 
morphology
The chemical characterisation of anaerobic sludge at 0 
days and final sludge at 1015 days from the reactors 
was conducted using FTIR spectroscopy (Figure 5).

4. Conclusions
The present study focused on the effect of micro-aera­
tion for enhancing the removal of organics and nutrients 
with a short HRT 6 h of anaerobic process with DO levels 
ranging from less than 1.0 mg/L in phase 1 and between 
1 and 1.5 mg/L in phase 2.
Significantly enhanced removal efficiency of organics 
and nutrients in the wastewater was observed. The 
removal of BOD, COD and TSS ranged from 80 to 90%, 
respectively at DO level <1.0 mg/L with continuous aera­
tion. A batch study refers to the growth of the microbiota 
responsible for the removal of nitrogen. Extended 
exposure to microaerobic conditions over a period of 
1015 days resulted in a progressive transformation of 
the microbiota. During all phases of study, sulphates 
were increased by more than 90% due to the sulphides 
oxidation after continuous aeration. The FTIR data 
suggested that organic molecules with phenolic O-H, N- 
H (proteins and peptides), and C=O vibration of alde­
hyde/carboxylic acid, respectively. The honeycomb-like 
structure shown in SEM pictures of reactor sludge 
further suggests that these structures are mostly associ­
ated with coccoid bacterial cells, most likely of NOBs and 
SOBs. Thus, micro-aerobic UASB reactors with integrated 
media have significant potential for scalable, efficient, 
and sustainable wastewater treatment, particularly in 
areas where energy, space, and operational simplicity are 
paramount. They signify a prospective advancement of 
anaerobic systems aimed at providing improved organic 
and nutrient removal with minimal added complexity.
